questions.q: Why did writing develop in Mesopotamia, and how was it done?

answer.text: Writing developed in Mesopotamia mainly out of the needs of city life and trade. As cities grew, there were countless transactions of goods, rations and taxes to be recorded, and human memory alone could not keep track of them. The earliest clay tablets carry lists of such records, showing that writing began as a means of keeping accounts.

The Mesopotamians wrote on tablets of wet clay using a sharp reed called a stylus, which made wedge-shaped marks. This script is therefore called cuneiform, from the Latin word for wedge. The tablets were dried in the sun and preserved. Writing was first in the Sumerian language and later in Akkadian.
In time writing spread from accounts to law, literature, prayers and administration, and being literate became a mark of prestige.

answer: Thus urban needs gave birth to one of the world's first writing systems.

questions.q: What was the importance of city life in Mesopotamian civilisation?
answer: City life was at the very heart of Mesopotamian civilisation and made possible its lasting achievements.

answer.text: In cities people no longer produced all their own needs. Some grew food, others made pots or cloth, and others traded. This division of labour and mutual interdependence made economic life more complex and productive.
Cities such as Uruk grew around temples, which organised trade and stored goods, and around markets that linked distant regions. The temple, or ziggurat, was the focus of religious and economic life.
Urban life created the need for record-keeping, giving rise to writing, and cities became centres of mathematics, astronomy and literature.

answer: Thus the city nourished the trade, writing and learning that define this early civilisation.

questions.q: How did the development of agriculture and cities transform early Mesopotamian society?

answer.text: saw one of the earliest shifts from village farming to city life, and this transformed society deeply.

list: A surplus of food from farming freed some people from producing food, letting them become craftsmen, priests, traders and officials
This division of labour and exchange gave rise to specialised occupations and trade
Large populations needed organisation, so rulers, temples and record-keeping developed
Wealth and status became unequal, and the temple and palace became centres of power and economic life

questions.q: What does Mesopotamian literature, including the Epic of Gilgamesh, tell us about their world?

answer.text: was used not only for records but for literature, which reveals how these people thought and felt.

list: The Epic of Gilgamesh, one of the world's oldest stories, tells of a king's search for immortality
It reflects on friendship, loss, and the human fear of death, showing a rich inner life
Myths and prayers reveal their religious beliefs and relationship with many gods
The preservation of these texts on clay tablets shows the value they placed on knowledge and learning
